messages.subject: Linkage mapping
messages.subject_clean: Linkage mapping
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm new to R/QTL and linkage mapping in general, so please bear with
me. I'm having problems using rqtl to assemble linkage maps using a
snp dataset containing 7327 snp loci that segregate among 20 progeny
of a female informative backcross (the female is the f1 of an
interspecific cross). My complete dataset is actually ~9300 snps for
30 progeny but I filtered out some individuals and loci that had large
amounts of missing data. Using the reduced dataset, 91% of genotypes
are present. I should mention that the female-informative cross was
intentional as there is no recombination during oogenesis in these
species meaning that any loci on the same chromosome will be
completely linked.

I've been using the tutorial to go through the process of assigning
loci to LGs but when I get to the formlinkagegroups step the
distribution of the loci end up being highly skewed so that a large
portion end up on one LG and each of the remaining loci appear singly
on other LGs (i've tried a range of different max.rf values and
min.lod scores). It doesn't make sense to have ~6000 snps on one LG
and ~1300 others all on different LGs. Also, there should only be 30
LGs. The potential issues I run into along the way are an initial
warning stating that "some chromosomes > 1000 cM...", a lot of
duplicate markers during the finddupmarkers step (which I haven't
filtered out because the tutorial doesn't cover this and I haven't
read into rqtl enough), and i get a about 30 or so loci that may have
switched alleles during the checkalleles step (after using markerlrt
but not with est.rf). Also, the frequency of homozygote genotypes is
about 3x as much as the frequency of heterozygote genotypes giving a
3:1 ratio (this should be about a 1:1 for a backcross).

I initially assumed that the issue was due to the segregation
distortion I was seeing in the genotype frequencies but after using an
even further reduced dataset of ~2000 loci that were selected for
their more even ratio of homozygotes to heterozygotes, I still
encounter the problem.

Currently, I'm at a loss as I do not know how to proceed.

Any help would be wonderful!

Thanks,

Bryan

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Substituting a Reference Genetic Map for a given Actual Genetic Map
messages.body_plain:
Regarding your first question, I would aim to get the true marker order for your cross, which would hopefully be the same between the two maps.  I would use the map that you think best reflects the underlying marker order.  Regarding distances, if you have reasonably dense marker genotype data (as you seem to, then it shouldn't matter whether you use the reference map or that estimated from your data.  And so I would focus on the results: do the analysis both ways, and then if the results are similar, use whatever map is convenient.  If the results are quite different, figure out which one you trust.

Regarding your second question, est.rf completely ignores the genetic map and just estimates recombination fraction between pairs of markers with the observed data.  But in my view this tool is solely for diagnostic purposes, and so I wouldn't worry about inconsistencies between the results from est.rf and your reference map.  But perhaps I'm not understanding your concern.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] mqmaugment()
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] mqmaugment()
messages.body_plain:
I'm not an expert on the details of MQM, but as I understand it, mqmaugment will augment the cross with multiple versions of each individual with all possible filled in genotypes, and these are then weighted according to their probabilities.  This approach handles the uncertainty in the imputed genotypes in the right way, and so should not make you too nervous.

fill.geno, on the other hand, by default replaces all missing data with a single imputation; subsequent analyses would then ignore the uncertainty in those imputed genotypes.

The cim() function in R/qtl is not better.  It calls fill.geno to do a single imputation and then ignores the uncertainty in those imputed genotypes, when it is identifying marker cofactors by forward selection.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Merging Rdata (scantwo permutation data) files
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Merging Rdata (scantwo permutation data) files
messages.body_plain:
There's an example of this on page 223 in the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org).

You just need to use c() to combine the multiple batches of permutations into a single object.  I generally do something like this:

if(exists("operm")) rm(operm)
for(i in 1:10) {
  attach(paste("file", i, ".RData"))
  if(i==1) op <- operm
  else op <- c(op, operm)
  detach(2)
}
operm <- op
rm(op)

Here I assume that the files are file1.RData, file2.RData, ..., file10.RData, and that they each contain a single object, "operm"
The first line makes sure that there's not already an object named "operm" in your workspace.

An important issue to consider is that the multiple permutation runs need to be started with different random "seeds"; I use set.seed() for this.

karl

R/qtl users:

I have been using Karl's PDF tutorial on genetic map contruction with regard to my RILself population and, as Karl sez in the tutorial, it is indeed "fun"!

But I have now hit a wall due to my lack of R software command experience.

There are some duplicate RIL pairs in my large RIL pop, and I would like retain the one member of each pair that has the fewest missing values (dashes).  In the tutorial, one member of an indentical pair of F2 individuals is dropped with the following cmds:
cg <- comparegeno(mapthis)
hist(cg[lower.tri(cg)], breaks=seq(0, 1, len=101), xlab="No. matching genotypes")
rug(cg[lower.tri(cg)])
wh <- which(cg > 0.9, arr=TRUE)
wh <- wh[wh[,1] < wh[,2],]
wh
mapthis <- subset(mapthis, ind=-wh[,2])

but it is the 2nd (random) member of each listed pair that is dropped, which may or may not be the one with the fewest missing genotypes.  The pull.geno and table cmds for RIL data display only an A and B genotype matrix (no missing cells in that matrix).  Any idea on how I could alter the above cmds to (automatically, if possible) drop the "less informative" member (the one with the most total missing values) of each identical RIL pair?

Yes, it can take a very long time.

Using n.cluster will distribute the map estimation of individual chromosomes to the multiple CPUs, but doesn't help to speed up the calculations on a given chromosome.

I will often consider a single selected chromosome and use the argument verbose=2 so that I can monitor convergence.  If you make the argument 'tol' a larger number (say 0.01), it will halt earlier (though with less precise estimates).

recombination fraction showed that I don't have marker pairs with
large LOD scores but RF >> 1/2. The genotype frequency plot and
histogram of number of matching genotypes b/w pairs of individuals
also came out as expected. We omitted some markers and individuals
that had lots of missing data. (I can show you our plots if you'd
like), but there is still a scattering of missing data throughout our
data set. I did get this warning message from summary.cross(): Some

messages.body_plain:
subset applied to a cross will only pull out selected chromosomes (or individuals), not phenotypes.

data.chr3 <- subset(data, chr=3)

If you want to retain just a given phenotype, you could use

data.chr3$pheno <- data.chr3$pheno[,2,drop=FALSE]

The drop=FALSE part ensures that it stays a data frame.

But effectplot() takes a phenotype column as an argument (pheno.col), as well as marker names, and so you shouldn't need to subset in advance.  Try something like

for(i in markernames(data, chr=3))
  effectplot(data, pheno.col=2, mname1=i)

It's best to not call your data "data", since that would disable the data() function.

Also consider the function effectscan:

effectscan(data, pheno.col=2, chr=3)

karl

ps  I'm not at my computer, and so I haven't tested the code above; there may be typos.

messages.body_plain:
If you have a number of intercrosses from inbred lines, you can tack them all together and load them as one cross, or you could load them separately and then combine them with the c() function.  (Formally, it'd call the c.cross function.)

That parental genotypes are important suggests that these are crosses among outbreds.  In that case they'd need to be treated as phase-known 4-way crosses.  You need to figure out phase first (which is hard if you don't have a map.)  And then you'd need to encode the genotypes in a special way (it's briefly explained in the help file for read.cross).  Analysis of four-way crosses is not well documented and can be quite tricky.  Unfortunately, R/qtl doesn't contain all of the necessary tools for constructing maps with outbred crosses.

karl
